The first leg of her tour begins with a visit to Moldova on Monday, marking the first-ever visit by an Indian President to the Eastern European nation. Shortly after her departure, the Rashtrapati Bhavan posted a message on X, saying, “President Droupadi Murmu embarks on state visits to the Republic of Moldova, the Republic of North Macedonia and Romania.” “This is the first-ever visit by an Indian President to Moldova and North Macedonia. The visit to Romania by the President of India is taking place after a gap of over three decades,” it said. Murmu will hold delegation-level talks with Moldovan President Maia Sandu and meet the President of the Parliament, Igor Grosu. She is also scheduled to interact with members of the Moldova-India Parliamentary Friendship Group, address a Business Forum, and meet with members of the Indian community. Photograph: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Terry Strada, center, who lost her husband Tom Strada, stands with others who lost loved ones in the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks listens during a press conference about the September 11th Transparency Act on Capitol Hill on 5 August 2021, in Washington DC. Photograph: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty Images September 11 2001 Victim families say it has ‘taken way too long’ to hold Saudi Arabia accountable for alleged support on 9/11 Terry Strada, whose husband was killed in the attacks, says she remains hopeful for justice as a lawsuit alleging Saudi support for the hijackers moves toward trial Ramon Antonio Vargas Thu 10 Sep 2026 14.37 EDT Last modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 15.27 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The leader of one group of 9/11 victims’ families says it has “taken way too long” to hold Saudi Arabia accountable for its alleged support of the terrorists who carried out the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks, whose 25th anniversary is being observed across the US on Friday. As that grim milestone approached, Terry Strada – the national chair of 9/11 Families United – said she felt as if it had “been several lifetimes” for there to be progress in the effort “to achieve a modicum of justice through our court system” in connection with the deadliest act of terror against the US. But, even as the Saudis deny they had any role in 9/11, she added that she was as hopeful as ever that “the day of reckoning will come”. “We will have it,” she said. Strada’s role with 9/11 Families stems from the death of her husband, Tom, when terrorists intentionally crashed hijacked airliners into New York City’s World Trade Center, the Pentagon in Washington DC and a field in Pennsylvania, killing nearly 3,000 people. Tom Strada, 41, was killed at the World Trade Center, widowing Terry, with whom he had three children – including one who was less than a week old. Terry Strada subsequently became an advocate for people who lost loved ones on September 11 and wanted to be made as whole as possible in its aftermath. She said “getting to the truth and understanding everything” about how her husband was killed was not only the best way she could think of to honor his memory – but to also protect their country. One of the 9/11 families’ most visible attempts at accountability for the attacks has been a years-long civil lawsuit alleging that Saudi Arabia supported the al-Qaida terror group operatives who carried out September 11. ‘Institutional neglect’: 25 years on from 9/11, experts sound alarm over US counter-terror efforts Read more Attorneys for Saudi Arabia have denied the lawsuit’s merits, maintaining that the kingdom has helped the US combat al-Qaida, its late founder Osama bin Laden, and terrorism in general. But in an August 2025 decision that Strada at the time called “another powerful step toward justice”, a federal judge in New York rejected a Saudi effort to dismiss the plaintiffs’ claims against the kingdom. The judge, George B Daniels, wrote in a legal opinion that an imam and an accountant’s employment by Saudi Arabia probably had links to their support of two al-Qaida members who came to the US in early 2000 to study English and take flight lessons. In his opinion, Daniels said that made the plaintiffs’ claims legally sufficient to proceed to trial, though it had not taken place as of Thursday. Other defendants named in the litigation – including al-Qaida itself, the Taliban and Iran – have already been found in default after not engaging with the claims. Regardless, as Friday loomed four days after celebrating her youngest son’s 25th birthday, Strada called on Saudi Arabia to “stop lying and take responsibility”. ABC News days earlier had reported on recently revealed records purportedly bolstering claims of Saudi complicity in 9/11. The outlet reported that those records included an alleged video of a kingdom agent casing the US Capitol, which investigators believe was the target of the airliner that crashed in Pennsylvania – and a sketch with calculations for flying a plane toward a ground target. Evidence of that kind was “strong”, Strada said. “You can’t deny it – and we are only getting more of it.” Nonetheless, the push to try that lawsuit has only been part of the focus for Strada’s advocacy alongside other kinds of 9/11 victims. Strada said she and many others collectively have spent years tracking the proceedings against a group of men who have spent years incarcerated at the US’s Guantánamo Bay detention camp for their alleged roles in the 9/11 attacks. She said she could hardly believe they were only recently given a tentative June 2028 trial date. Meanwhile, Strada was also a prominent voice against LIV Golf, the breakaway tour that was backed by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, which was launched in 2022 and spent billions of dollars luring players away from the US-based PGA. One professional US golfer who joined the LIV tour, Brooks Koepka, was asked what he would tell the families of 9/11 victims about his getting into business with a Saudi venture. He replied, in part, “I think as we move forward from that, we have to look toward the pathway to peace and forgiveness.” Strada and her allies disagreed with that kind of sentiment. “These people don’t understand how devastating September 11 was,” Strada said at the time. “My husband was dismembered. We don’t know where all his body parts landed. He has never been identified. “There was a psychological cruel[ty] that people do not realize.” All of which has made it a relief for Strada, she said in a moment of honesty, to see LIV Golf enduring deep financial struggles ahead of Friday. The tour filed for federal bankruptcy protection in her home state of New Jersey after abruptly losing its wealthy Saudi investors months earlier. Accusing them of “ sportswashing ”, Strada said, “The Saudis … [were] trying to improve their image and have a younger generation view them in a different way. And it didn’t work. There is some satisfaction in that.” Explore more on these topics September 11 2001 New Jersey New York Saudi Arabia Al-Qaida news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

Photograph: Will Oliver/EPA US politics Democratic senator says Hegseth trying to hide costs of Iran war from US public Chris Murphy says Pentagon blocked him from military base in Qatar and Iran strike on US embassy in Riyadh far worse than public led to believe Joseph Gedeon in Washington Thu 8 Oct 2026 17.41 EDT Last modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 18.33 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Senator Chris Murphy said the Pentagon blocked him from a major US base in Qatar, yet saw enough damage on the US embassy in Saudi Arabia to conclude that an Iranian strike would have been deadly had it happened during the day. The Connecticut Democrat, who sits on the Senate foreign relations and appropriations committees, described the destruction he witnessed in Riyadh as “extraordinary” and much more damaging than the public has been led to believe. “Had that attack happened during the daytime, there’s no doubt that there would have been many, many Americans killed,” he told reporters on a call after returning from Qatar and Saudi Arabia. He also accused the Pentagon of trying to prevent Congress from seeing the costs of the war first-hand, saying the Pentagon secretary, Pete Hegseth , was “determined to hide the cost and the consequences of this war from the American public”. Two drones hit the compound in the early hours of 3 March, days after the US and Israel launched the war on 28 February, setting off a fire and sending black smoke over the district. The building was reportedly empty at the time and no injuries were reported. Saudi Arabia’s defense ministry initially described the damage as minor. But, according to Murphy, the drones caused extensive damage across several floors. The strike, he explained, hit “an area of the embassy in which there are a lot of people” and said that “part of that space is uninhabitable and will likely remain uninhabitable”. Murphy said some of it would not be repaired because the embassy is moving soon. In Qatar, the senator visited Ras Laffan, the gas complex where Iranian drone strikes halted LNG (liquefied natural gas) production early in the war. Murphy said 17% of Qatar’s exports had been eliminated, probably for at least three years of repairs. He also said he saw just one LNG tanker in port, compared with the usual six, and about one a day leaving rather than 10. Murphy said the Pentagon blocked him from seeing more. He said he gave notice of his visit weeks in advance and submitted a written request for access to Al Udeid air base, the largest US military installation in the region. He also said he raised it with Adm Brad Cooper, the commander of the US Central Command, who appeared surprised that military leaders had also been barred from speaking to him. On arrival, Murphy said, he was told he would not have access to the base and no contact with military leadership. In response, a senior Pentagon official told the Guardian that Murphy’s office “was informed before his trip” that he would not receive department support to access Al Udeid air base, as per Hegseth’s 3 March directive on travel restrictions in the region. “That decision was communicated in advance by the office of the secretary of war for legislative affairs,” the official said in a statement. “The department applies the secretary’s guidance evenly.” Murphy said he would draft language in the coming days requiring the Pentagon to give members of Congress access to overseas bases, which he would seek to include in next year’s appropriations and defense authorization bills. If the war is still going by early next year, he said Congress should withhold defense funding unless it includes a provision to end the conflict, and vowed accountability and investigations if Democrats win one or both chambers in next month’s midterm elections. The administration, he said, was “giving its middle finger to the Congress, pretending as if we are totally irrelevant”. “We will potentially have power of both the House and the Senate,” Murphy said of Democrats, “and we should make the end of the war a priority.” Explore more on these topics US politics US military Democrats US-Israel war on Iran Pete Hegseth news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

( ) By Newsfile October 4, 2026 at 12:19 p.m. Beijing, China–(Newsfile Corp. – October 4, 2026) – The documentary film The Panda Adventure will air simultaneously on ERT1, Greece’s national television channel, and MEGA, a mainstream commercial television channel, on Oct. 28. With this, the “Charming Beijing” documentary showcase have now reached nine countries. Five documentaries produced by BRTV—The Forbidden City, Changcheng Chang (The Great Wall’s Vast Stretch), The Panda Adventure, Beijing Central Axis-The Legend of A Line and Letters from Beijing Swift—have been translated into multiple languages and broadcast successively on mainstream television channels in countries across Asia, Latin America and Europe. As of September, all episodes had been aired in Indonesia, India, Brazil and Hungary, achieving a cumulative overseas audience reach of approximately 15 million. Changcheng Chang aired a total of 20 episodes on DD Bihar in India and TVRI in Indonesia, marking the documentary’s debut on India’s national television network. Beijing Central Axis-The Legend of A Line was broadcast on Brazil’s national television network, with potential coverage of nearly 200 million viewers through local public broadcasting and free-to-air digital television networks. After The Panda Adventure aired in Hungary, it reached more than 930,000 viewers, according to figures from the broadcaster. The broadcaster also forwarded 20 letters from viewers, all expressing positive feedback. The five documentaries present Beijing from different perspectives: its palaces, the Great Wall, giant pandas, the Central Axis and Beijing swifts. Online, related content has generated more than 12 million views in total, including 5.943 million views for a single post announcing the premiere of Changcheng Chang . On Oct. 27, a “Charming Beijing” cultural event will kick off in Athens, building anticipation ahead of the television broadcast.
